title: A Wound That Will Be Healed
overview: The LORD promises that his scattered and badly wounded people, punished for their wrongs, will one day be brought home, healed and given a ruler of their own.

parts.label: Write it down (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Jeremiah is told to record these promises in a scroll, so later generations could compare them with what actually happened. Israel here means the northern tribes taken away by Assyria long before, and Judah the southern kingdom now facing exile in Babylon.

parts.label: A day of terror (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: The scene is so frightening that even strong men clutch their stomachs like women giving birth, their faces drained of color. Many readers note that labor pain ends in new life, which fits the promise that Jacob, meaning the whole nation, will come through it.

parts.label: Freedom and a new David (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: The yoke is foreign rule, and David their king means a future ruler from David's family, since David had died long before; Christians read this as pointing to Jesus. The nations that scattered Israel will come to an end, but Israel will not, though it will still be disciplined in fair measure.

parts.label: An injury beyond healing (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: The nation is pictured as a wound no medicine can fix, abandoned by former allies, probably neighbors such as Egypt. The text says bluntly that the LORD struck them like a cruel enemy because of their many sins.

parts.label: Healing for the outcast (vv. 16-22)
parts.note: Because others mock Zion, meaning Jerusalem, as a castoff no one wants, the LORD promises to heal it, rebuild the city on its old site and give it a ruler from its own people. This ruler will dare to come close to God, something thought too dangerous for most people, and the old bond is restated: you will be my people, and I will be your God.

parts.label: The storm of the LORD (vv. 23-24)
parts.note: These lines repeat an earlier warning from Jeremiah 23, here seemingly aimed at the wicked who harmed God's people. Scholars are unsure exactly how they fit, but they say God's purpose will be carried out and only understood later.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether these promises were fulfilled in the return from Babylon, still await a future literal restoration of Israel, or find their main fulfillment in Jesus and the community gathered around him.
think: Can a person be honest that some suffering grew out of their own choices and still believe they deserve to be healed?
